faq.a: Because creatinine only rises after ~50 % loss of GFR; early disease is compensated.
faq.q: Why can serum creatinine be normal in early CKD?

faq.a: Pre‑renal azotemia from volume depletion or low perfusion.
faq.q: What does a BUN/creatinine ratio > 20 indicate?

faq.a: Refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary oedema, or uremic encephalopathy.
faq.q: When is dialysis indicated in AKI?

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with malaria presents with oliguria and creatinine 2.8 mg/dL – what is your next step? — Assess volume status, give cautious IV fluids, and order urine microscopy to differentiate pre‑renal from intrinsic AKI.
How does a patient with sickle‑cell disease develop CKD? — Repeated vaso‑occlusive infarcts cause papillary necrosis and chronic ischemia, leading to progressive GFR loss.
Why is a BUN/creatinine ratio unreliable in a malnourished patient? — Low protein intake reduces BUN production, masking pre‑renal azotemia.
What ultrasound finding would change management of a patient with rising creatinine? — Detecting hydronephrosis prompts urgent relief of obstruction (catheter or stent).

Explain why ACE‑I/ARB are first‑line in proteinuric CKD but avoided in bilateral renal artery stenosis. — They reduce intraglomerular pressure and protein loss; in bilateral stenosis they can precipitate AKI by dropping GFR.
A patient on herbal tea develops AKI; what toxin is most likely? — Aristolochic acid from certain traditional herbs causes interstitial nephritis and rapid GFR decline.
How would you manage hyperkalaemia when ECG shows peaked T waves? — Give IV calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, consider nebulised beta‑agonist, and arrange urgent dialysis if refractory.
What distinguishes acute tubular necrosis from acute interstitial nephritis on urine microscopy? — ATN shows muddy brown granular casts; AIN shows white blood cell casts and eosinophils.
ai.title: Renal Function Assessment
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Understanding how kidneys filter blood, maintain fluid/electrolyte balance, and excrete waste is essential for diagnosing acute and chronic kidney disease, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: GFR reflects filtration capacity; normal ≈ 90–120 mL/min/1.73 m².
Serum creatinine rises only after ~50 % loss of GFR.
sections.p: The kidneys filter ~180 L of plasma daily, reabsorb needed substances, and excrete waste. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the key measure of renal function.

b: GFR estimation uses creatinine‑based equations (CKD‑EPI, MDRD).
Urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for > 6 h signals acute kidney injury (AKI).
sections.p: Renal function is evaluated by filtration (GFR), tubular handling (reabsorption, secretion), and endocrine roles (EPO, renin).

b: AKI: rapid rise in creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or ≥1.5× baseline.
CKD: GFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months.
sections.p: Kidney dysfunction presents with oliguria, edema, electrolyte disturbances, and uremic symptoms. In low‑resource hospitals, common causes include dehydration, severe infections, nephrotoxic herbs, and sickle‑cell nephropathy.

t.b: What is the current GFR? – Elevated creatinine indicates reduced filtration; use equation to estimate GFR.
Is there pre‑renal azotemia? – BUN/creatinine > 20 suggests volume depletion.
Is there glomerular injury? – Protein ≥1+ or hematuria points to glomerulonephritis.
What is the cause of AKI? – Muddy brown casts = acute tubular necrosis; RBC casts = glomerulonephritis.
Is obstruction present? – Dilated pelvicalyceal system suggests obstructive uropathy.
What metabolic derangements exist? – Hyperkalaemia > 5.5 mmol/L signals need urgent treatment.

b: Rehydrate cautiously in pre‑renal AKI; avoid fluid overload.
Stop nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, herbal remedies).
Use loop diuretics for volume overload when GFR > 15 mL/min.
Treat hyperkalaemia with calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, and consider dialysis if > 6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes.
In CKD, control blood pressure (ACE‑I/ARB) and treat anemia with erythropoietin when Hb < 10 g/dL.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect remaining nephrons, and correct fluid/electrolyte derangements.

b: Relying on a single creatinine value without baseline.
Assuming normal BUN rules out AKI; BUN may be low in malnutrition.
Giving diuretics before assessing volume status.
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from misinterpreting labs or ignoring context.

b: Link oliguria with possible pre‑renal causes in dehydrated malaria patients.
Differentiate AKI from CKD using timeline and ultrasound findings.
sections.p: Examiners test integration of history, exam, and investigations.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden anuria or oliguria with rising creatinine
Pulmonary oedema or severe hypertension in CKD
